1240.title: Languages of the court
1240.hook: he wrote in Braj, Persian and Punjabi
1240.howItsDone: Sikhs recite Guru Gobind Singh's compositions in their original languages, Braj, Persian and Punjabi, usually printed in Gurmukhi script, and teachers explain them in katha in Punjabi, English and other languages.

segments.voice: Yesterday, names of weapons: a garland of blades used to name the power that protects. Your line was tools for good.

Over the last two weeks, the readings have quietly changed language underfoot. The letter to the emperor: Persian. The war ballad whose first lines open the Ardas: Punjabi. The swayyas, the praise of the Khalsa, the garland of weapon names: mostly Braj, a literary language of poets in northern India. Three languages, one writer. That's not an accident of translation. Readers see a choice in it, a tongue for each job, and today is about why that matters.
screen: `THE LETTER: PERSIAN.` → `THE BALLAD: PUNJABI.` → `THE POEMS: MOSTLY BRAJ.`

segments.voice: Day eighty-three named these three languages; today, why. Each language is a door into a different room. Persian was the language of the Mughal court, of government and letters between powers. So the letter to the emperor went in Persian verse, the language its reader worked in every day. Punjabi was the language of the people at home, of the fields and villages. A var, a ballad of courage, belongs there, so Chandi di Var is in Punjabi, the tongue its listeners breathed in. Braj was the language of poetry across a wide stretch of northern India, the one poets used for devotion and for story. Much of the Guru's longer poetry is in Braj, written in the Gurmukhi script. Jaap Sahib, one of the Sikh morning prayers, is full of names for God, and some readers notice that it draws them from more than one world. Alongside names rooted in Sanskrit, it calls God Razak, the provider, and Rahim, the merciful, words that come from Arabic and Persian. It's the move Akal Ustat and the Zafarnama's opening made, carried into a daily prayer. One God, praised in the vocabularies of neighbors who often didn't share a prayer. For Sikhs that fits a long thread. The Guru Granth Sahib itself gathers voices from many regions and backgrounds. Many tongues, one Name. Language, in this tradition, isn't a fence around the holy. It's a set of doors, and the Guru walked through several of them.
screen: `PERSIAN: THE LANGUAGE OF THE COURT.` · `PUNJABI: THE LANGUAGE OF HOME.` · `BRAJ: THE LANGUAGE OF POETS.` · `ONE GOD, MANY VOCABULARIES.` · then, large: `MANY TONGUES.`

segments.voice: Pick a word you know in a language that isn't your first, thank you, peace, water, and say it once, quietly, noticing how it sits in your mouth. Then bring to mind the people who say that word every day without thinking, and let them be near for a breath or two; if you pray, follow the word with Waheguru.

1241.title: The poets of Anandpur
1241.hook: tradition says he kept dozens of poets at his court
1241.howItsDone: Sikhs sing the Persian ghazals of Bhai Nand Lal Goya in kirtan, and Sikh tradition remembers Guru Gobind Singh's Anandpur as a center where poets and scholars translated and wrote.

segments.voice: Yesterday, languages of the court: Persian for the emperor, Punjabi for the people, Braj for poetry. Your line was many tongues.

Anandpur, in the hills. A town under threat for years, drilling soldiers, storing grain, watching the passes. And in the middle of it, tradition says, a room full of poets. Dozens of them, gathered by Guru Gobind Singh, writing, translating, reciting. Under pressure, the extras usually get cut first. The Guru, by this memory, did the opposite. You first visited this court on day eighty-three. Today is about that court, and about one poet whose words are still sung.
screen: `A TOWN UNDER THREAT.` → `A ROOM FULL OF POETS.` → `THE OPPOSITE OF CUTTING EXTRAS.`

segments.voice: Sikh tradition remembers the poets of Anandpur as a gathering of writers from different backgrounds: Sikhs and others, scholars of Sanskrit and of Persian. Tradition says the Guru set them to work bringing older works of story and wisdom into Braj, so that ordinary people could reach what had been locked in learned languages. Tradition also tells of a great collection of this work, sometimes called Vidya Sagar, the ocean of learning, and says much of it was lost in the flooded Sarsa river when Anandpur was left. Nobody now can read what went under. One poet's work did survive, and Sikhs still sing it. Bhai Nand Lal, called Goya, wrote in Persian, ghazals and couplets of love for the Guru. Paraphrased, he writes of the Guru's face as the thing he longs to see, and of a single glance from the Guru being worth more than the world. Sikh practice gives his poems a place in kirtan, alongside the Gurus' own hymns. Why would a Guru at war keep poets? Some readers answer: because what he was defending was not only land. It was a way of life, and a way of life needs songs, stories and learning to carry it. Swords protect a people; poems tell them who they are. The court of poets was the second half of the defense.

1242.title: The rehatnamas
1242.hook: codes of conduct linked to the Tenth Guru's time, written down by Sikhs after him
1242.howItsDone: Sikh historians and teachers read the rehatnamas as early records of Sikh discipline; for daily practice, gurdwaras and Sikh families follow the Sikh Rehat Maryada, a shared code drawn up later.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the poets of Anandpur: a Guru under threat who, tradition says, still kept a court of writers, and Bhai Nand Lal's Persian poems, still sung. Your line was a court of poets.

A family keeps a list on the fridge. Shoes off at the door. Nobody eats until everyone sits. Say thank you to whoever cooked. Nobody voted on it, exactly. It grew out of how the family wanted to live, and somebody finally wrote it down. After the Tenth Guru, Sikhs wrote down lists like that, on a much larger scale: what to do at dawn, how to treat a guest, what to give, what to avoid.
screen: `A LIST ON THE FRIDGE.` → `HOW WE WANT TO LIVE, WRITTEN DOWN.` → `CODES OF HOW A SIKH SHOULD LIVE.`

segments.voice: The word is rehatnama. Rehat is a way of living, a discipline kept day after day. Nama is a written piece, a letter or a record. Together: a written code for living. Tradition links these codes to the circle around Guru Gobind Singh. Some carry the names of Sikhs remembered as close to him; one is linked with Bhai Nand Lal, remembered as a poet of the Guru's court. They were written down after the Guru's time, and that matters for how they're read. They are not scripture. They sit beside the Guru Granth Sahib, not inside it. What do they hold? Mostly ordinary things, which is the point. Rise early. Remember the Name. Bathe and recite the morning prayers. Share what you earn. Keep the hair uncut. Treat the Guru's word with honor. For the Sikhs who wrote them, faith was not only an inner feeling. It was a shape for the whole day. Here's the honest part. The rehatnamas don't all say the same thing. They differ in detail, and some hold lines that later Sikhs questioned or set aside. Scholars and Sikh bodies have read them side by side, and out of that long conversation came a shared code you'll meet later on the path, the Sikh Rehat Maryada. So a rehatnama is a window, not a final word: early Sikhs putting the Gurus' teaching into daily life, written down by people who cared enough to try.

1243.title: His letters
1243.hook: his hukamnamas to sangats ask for offerings, weapons and faithfulness
1243.howItsDone: Surviving hukamnamas of the Gurus are kept by families and gurdwaras and are sometimes displayed for the sangat; separately, gurdwaras read a daily hukamnama from the Guru Granth Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the rehatnama: codes of daily Sikh living, written down after the Tenth Guru and read side by side. Your line was a code for living.

A rider arrives in a far town with a folded paper. The Sikhs there gather in the dharamsal, the place where they meet to sing. Someone unfolds it and reads it aloud. It's from the Guru. It names them, the whole sangat of that town, and speaks to them directly. It asks them for things. It promises them something. Then it's folded again and kept, carefully, by people who will hand it to their children. Letters like that survive.
screen: `A RIDER WITH A FOLDED PAPER.` → `READ ALOUD TO THE WHOLE SANGAT.` → `KEPT AND HANDED DOWN.`

segments.voice: They're called hukamnamas. Hukam means an order or a command; nama, as yesterday, is a written piece. So a hukamnama is a written order. Some letters of Guru Gobind Singh are preserved by Sikh families and gurdwaras, and scholars have gathered and studied them. They ask for three kinds of things. First, offerings: sangats should send what they've set aside for the Guru, and tradition says some tell them to send it straight to him, not through the old middlemen, the masands. Second, weapons and horses, because the Guru's community at Anandpur needed to defend itself. Third, under everything, faithfulness. Come to the Guru. Keep his teaching. Stay close. Notice the tone. These aren't cold decrees. The letters speak to whole communities as the Guru's own, and tradition says some carry a promise of care, that the Guru will look after them. A command, yes, but one that sounds like family writing home. One word nearby is easy to mix up. In a gurdwara, the hymn read from the opened Guru Granth Sahib is also called the hukamnama, the day's order. Today means something else: the Tenth Guru's own letters, written to his Sikhs in their towns. Put the two side by side and a picture appears. The Guru speaks and the sangat listens, whether the words arrive on horseback or from an open page.

1244.title: The white hawk
1244.hook: tradition remembers him with a white hawk and a blue horse
1244.howItsDone: Sikh paintings, calendars and devotional songs show Guru Gobind Singh on a blue horse with a white hawk, and Sikhs call him by these images in song.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Tenth Guru's letters: hukamnamas asking far-off sangats for offerings, arms and faithfulness. Your line was a guru's letters.

Look at a Sikh painting of Guru Gobind Singh, on a kitchen calendar, a gurdwara wall, an old book. Often he's on horseback, and the horse is blue-gray. On his raised, gloved hand sits a white hawk. Sikh songs call him by those two things: in Punjabi, the one with the white hawk, the rider of the blue horse. A teacher remembered by a bird and a horse. Why?
screen: `A PAINTING ON A KITCHEN WALL.` → `A BLUE HORSE, A WHITE HAWK.` → `REMEMBERED BY A BIRD.`

segments.voice: Start with the plain meaning. In the Guru's world, a trained hawk on the wrist belonged to rulers and nobles; hawking was a royal pastime. So a Guru with a hawk carries himself like a sovereign. That fits his own writings: a man who writes to an emperor as an equal and calls his followers to stand up straight, unafraid. Some Sikhs read the hawk as saying, without a word, this community bows only to God. Now the color. The songs dwell on the white, and some Sikhs hear it as purity: power held with a clean heart. The hawk is fierce, it hunts, but it comes back to the glove. Strength that answers to someone. Then the horse. Tradition gives him a blue horse, and the image runs straight into Sikh life. Blue is a color some Khalsa Sikhs wear in their turbans and robes, and the Nihang Sikhs, who keep the old martial ways, are known for it. Riders on horseback still lead some Sikh processions. Here's the honest line. These are memories carried in paintings, songs and stories, not details the Guru records about himself. Tradition holds them, and Sikhs treasure them. They give a face to an idea: a teacher of the One, mounted and ready, with a wild bird that chooses to come back to his hand.

1245.title: Nanded, the last days
1245.hook: tradition says he was stabbed by an assassin at Nanded and died of the wound
1245.howItsDone: Sikhs travel to Takht Sachkhand Sri Hazur Sahib at Nanded to remember the Tenth Guru's last days, and gurdwaras mark the anniversary of his passing with kirtan and Ardas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the white hawk and the blue horse: a sovereign bearing, kept alive in paintings and songs. Your line was the hawk and the horse.

A river in the south, the Godavari, far from Punjab. A town on its bank called Nanded. A great white gurdwara stands there now, and Sikhs travel a very long way to stand in it. Why so far from home? Because tradition says this is where the Tenth Guru's road ended. He had come south, a long way from Anandpur, and at Nanded he stopped. Sikhs tell what happened there gently, and that's how it's told here.
screen: `A RIVER IN THE SOUTH.` → `A TOWN CALLED NANDED.` → `WHERE THE ROAD ENDED.`

segments.voice: Tradition tells the last days in a few strokes. At Nanded, the Guru met an ascetic named Madho Das, living by the river. The meeting changed him. He became a Sikh, took the name Banda Singh, and the Guru sent him north to Punjab, a story for another day. Then came the blow. Tradition says an assassin, a Pathan, came near the Guru and stabbed him. The wound was dressed and stitched, and for a while it seemed he might recover. Then, the story goes, he drew a strong bow, and the stitches gave way. He knew his time was short. What he did with it is the part Sikhs hold closest. He did not name another person to follow him. Tradition says he gathered his Sikhs and placed the Guru's authority where it would stay; tomorrow looks at that carefully. Today, just notice the calm. A man who had lost his father, his mother and his four sons, who had fought and written and wandered, ends not in panic but in arranging what comes next. The place where he passed is now Takht Sachkhand Sri Hazur Sahib, one of the seats of authority in Sikh life. Sachkhand means the realm of truth, the last of the realms in Guru Nanak's Japji. So the name itself points past the earth. Nanded is where the line of human Gurus came to its close, and where a new way of being guided was about to begin.
screen: `MADHO DAS BECOMES BANDA SINGH.` · `THE ASSASSIN, AND THE WOUND.` · `CALM, ARRANGING WHAT COMES NEXT.` · `SACHKHAND: THE REALM OF TRUTH.` · then, large: `THE LAST DAYS.`

segments.voice: Let the bare outline of his life pass through your mind, the boy at Anandpur, the hawk, the letters, the losses, the long road south, the river at Nanded, and then let it go still. If you pray, sit in Waheguru for him; if not, sit in plain respect for a life given all the way to the end.

1246.hook: he left the Guru's authority to the scripture and to the Khalsa gathered before it

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nanded: the river town where, tradition says, the Tenth Guru's road ended, calm to the last. Your line was the last days.

Who comes next? Families ask it over a will. Companies ask it in a boardroom. For nearly every step of Sikh history so far, the answer had been a person: Guru Nanak passed the light to Guru Angad, and on down the line, ten Gurus in all. At Nanded, with his time running out, the Tenth Guru faced the same question. Sikhs remember his answer as a turning point. It wasn't a name.
screen: `WHO COMES NEXT?` → `ALWAYS, UNTIL NOW, A PERSON.` → `THIS TIME, NOT A NAME.`

segments.voice: Tradition says Guru Gobind Singh placed the Guru's authority in two places at once. First, the scripture. The book of the Gurus' hymns, the Adi Granth, would itself be the Guru from now on: the Guru Granth Sahib. Granth means a book, a volume. Second, the people. The Khalsa, the community of initiated Sikhs, gathered in the presence of that book, would carry the Guru's authority together: the Guru Panth. Panth means a path, and the people who walk it. A verse Sikhs sing after the Ardas, the common prayer, carries this memory. In paraphrase: by the command of the Timeless One the Panth was founded; let every Sikh accept the Granth as the Guru. The two halves fit. The book holds the word. The people, gathered before it, decide how to live it. Neither stands alone. That's why, in a gurdwara, the Guru Granth Sahib is treated as a living Guru, not a library book: opened in the morning under a canopy, a whisk waved over it, carried to rest at night. And it's why important matters for the Panth have been decided by Sikhs meeting together in the Guru's presence, sometimes through five chosen Sikhs who stand for the whole Khalsa. It's a bold answer. No single successor to argue over. No one person who could be bribed or killed. The word is fixed in a book anyone can open, and the authority to apply it belongs to a gathered community. The line of ten ends, and the Guru goes on.
screen: `THE BOOK BECOMES THE GURU.` · `THE GATHERED KHALSA, THE GURU PANTH.` · `THE WORD, AND THE PEOPLE WHO LIVE IT.` · `NO SINGLE SUCCESSOR TO FIGHT OVER.` · then, large: `THE BOOK AND THE PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: First the book: bring to mind words that have guided you, from any page that has mattered, and bow your head a little toward them. Then the people: picture the circle you belong to, family, friends, a congregation, and hold them with respect, and if you pray, say Waheguru once for each.
Guru Granth. The scripture as living Guru, given that authority, tradition says, by Guru Gobind Singh, alongside the gathered Khalsa, the Guru Panth. Today's word.
Your line: the book and the people. The word in one, the living of it in the other. Rest well.
